#4919. What the CFTC’s New Crypto Reserves Guidance Actually Allows—And What It Doesn’t

What the CFTC’s New Crypto Reserves Guidance Actually Allows—And What It Doesn’t

The U.S. derivatives regulator has quietly opened the door for crypto exchanges and clearinghouses to hold Bitcoin, Ethereum, and stablecoins as part of the financial cushion they’re required to keep, the latest sign of the agency weaving digital assets into the plumbing of regulated markets.

But the fine print matters, and it draws a careful line.

In a staff advisory issued this week, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s Division of Market Oversight and Division of Clearing and Risk explained how swap execution facilities, designated contract markets, and derivatives clearing organizations can use crypto assets to meet their financial-resources requirements.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Those rules require such platforms to hold enough resources to cover at least 12 months of operating costs, a buffer meant to ensure a venue can keep running or wind down safely if it hits trouble.

Here’s what the guidance allows: Certain crypto assets, specifically naming Bitcoin, Ethereum, and payment stablecoins, can now count toward that 12-month requirement, subject to “appropriate haircuts,” meaning their value would be discounted to account for volatility. That’s a meaningful concession, effectively recognizing crypto as a legitimate corporate reserve asset for the firms the CFTC oversees.

Here’s what it doesn’t allow, and this is the catch that defines the policy: Crypto can’t be counted toward a separate liquidity requirement.

Because digital assets don’t qualify as “cash” or “highly liquid securities” under Generally Accepted Accounting Principles, they fall short of that stricter test. In practice, a platform can hold Bitcoin or Ethereum as part of its longer-term financial backstop, but it still needs traditional cash-like instruments on hand to satisfy the rule meant to ensure it can pay obligations quickly.

The distinction is the whole point. It lets firms treat crypto as a store of value on their balance sheets while reinforcing that, when it comes to assets that must be instantly spendable, volatile tokens still don’t make the cut.

The nuance is easy to miss, but it reflects a measured posture from a regulator that has otherwise moved aggressively on crypto.

The CFTC has already previously cleared perpetual futures on individual stocks, issued no-action relief letting crypto apps offer regulated derivatives, and floated a plan to bring crypto exchanges under federal oversight, part of a broader push to set digital-asset policy on its own authority.

That said, it’s worth noting that the advisory represents the views of CFTC staff only. It creates no new rules or enforceable rights, isn’t a no-action position, and doesn’t necessarily reflect the views of the Commission itself.

It could also shift as the agency’s makeup changes. President Donald Trump recently sent a bipartisan slate of nominees to fill vacant CFTC and SEC seats, which could reshape the commissions now steering crypto policy.

For now, the guidance is best read not as crypto winning blanket acceptance as a reserve asset, but as the CFTC sorting out precisely where digital assets fit, and where they still don’t, in the machinery of regulated trading.

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 18, 2026 3:54 PM EST

UPDATE, November 19, 2026, 4:15 p.m. EST: Fiona the hippo has died.

Fiona the hippo remains under the watchful eyes of veterinarians and staff at the Cincinnati Zoo after swallowing a hat last week. As a full-grown hippo, surgery is not an option for Fiona, but her caretakers remain hopeful she will pass the foreign object naturally.

Last week, a knit hat entered her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo and the almost 10-year-old hippo ate it. Given her size, zookeepers initially thought she’d simply pass the hat, but it remains stuck in her digestive track. She has undergone a colonoscopy using a 9-foot scope and multiple ultrasounds that show intestinal bunching, indicating her body is continuing to try and expel the hat. Caretakers have continued to give her fluids and sedate her when necessary for tests.

“Fiona ingested an object that a visitor accidentally tossed into her habitat,” the Cincinnati Zoo said in a statement. “Our veterinary team and hippo care staff are monitoring her around the clock and doing everything they can to help her pass the object safely. Her care team is cautiously optimistic that she will pass it and return to her usual self. Fiona will remain off habitat until this is resolved. We will share updates as we have more information.”

The zoo also reminded patrons to be careful with their things when observing animals: “Please help us keep our animals safe by securing your belongings and taking extra care near habitats. Ingesting foreign objects can cause serious health problems for animals. If something falls into a habitat, please notify a Zoo staff member immediately.”

On Wednesday, November 18, the zoo shared a new approach in Fiona’s ongoing treatment: a vibration plate borrowed from a local Ohio horse farm. Fiona could be seen standing on the plate, vocalizing to caretakers. “The hope is that the vibrations will help encourage movement through her digestive tract and help the object pass,” the team explained.

Fiona first captured the internet’s heart in 2017, when she was born six weeks premature. Baby hippos typically weigh about 100 pounds at birth, but tiny Fiona tipped the scales at a mere 29 pounds. She was the smallest known hippo to survive such a low birth weight. As she grew, Fiona took social media and the real world by storm: she photobombed an engagement shoot, had a local ice cream named in her honor, and even starred in her own reality-TV series appropriately called “The Fiona Show.”  Her surprise baby brother Fritz was born in 2022, after their mother’s birth control went “on the fritz.”

#4914. Bitcoin Losses Are the Worst Since FTX. Is the Bottom Near?

Bitcoin Losses Are the Worst Since FTX. Is the Bottom Near?

Bitcoin investors are locking in their heaviest losses since the collapse of FTX in November 2022, according to a report published Tuesday by blockchain analytics firm Glassnode.

The world’s largest cryptocurrency slipped below $60,000, trading at $59,992, more than 50% from its October 2025 peak.

“Bitcoin losses are the heaviest since FTX,” Glassnode wrote on X. “Set against the money that flowed into Bitcoin over the past year, they have almost doubled in a week.”

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Glassnode tracks realized losses by looking at coins that move on-chain at prices lower than when they previously moved. Measuring those losses against the capital that entered Bitcoin over the preceding year gives analysts a way to compare sell-offs across market cycles, even as the cryptocurrency grows in value.

The last time the indicator reached these levels, Sam Bankman-Fried’s crypto empire was collapsing and Bitcoin was trading below $16,000. This time, the selling pressure has coincided with a much broader retreat from risky assets, and even good news for the tech industry hasn’t been enough to keep Bitcoin afloat.

Bitcoin rallied 5% in about half an hour on Monday after Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang was returning as CEO. Less than six hours later, Bitcoin had given back the entire rally, while the Nasdaq 100 still held roughly three-quarters of its gains. In trading, this is known as a bull trap, and happens on strong bearish trends.

Bitcoin’s correlation with the Nasdaq 100 is now at its highest since September 2022, Glassnode said. Over the past 60 trading days, Bitcoin has tended to gain less when tech stocks rise and lose more when they fall.

U.S. investors have also been pulling money out of the market. Spot Bitcoin ETFs have lost $4.3 billion on net over the past 20 trading days, while Coinbase traders have been heavy net sellers over the past month. Buying and selling on Binance, meanwhile, have been roughly balanced.

“Spikes like this often came close to past lows, but some came early,” Glassnode said. The firm pointed to the sell-offs of early 2019, March 2020, and November 2022, when losses surged near market bottoms, but also to earlier episodes in 2018 and 2022 when prices had further to fall.

Long-term holders—investors who have held their coins for roughly five months or longer—accounted for most realized losses from mid-April to mid-November. Nearly 90% of the long futures positions vulnerable to liquidation between last week’s Bitcoin price and $53,200 are also gone, reducing the potential for another cascade of forced selling within that range.

Glassnode is watching Bitcoin’s realized price, the average price at which circulating coins last moved, which currently stands at $53,200. Bitcoin traded below that metric before bottoming in each of the previous three major bear markets.

Applying the discounts seen at the lows of 2022 and 2018 to today’s realized price would put Bitcoin at roughly $41,000 and $37,000, respectively.

For now, the more immediate concern is whether Bitcoin can close above its June closing low of $58,500. Glassnode said a recovery above $60,000 accompanied by renewed ETF inflows would help establish whether the summer lows are holding.

#4912. I finally got a USB-C charging e-bike, and it costs 75% less than Rivian’s bike

I’ve been waiting years for electric bikes to finally embrace USB-C charging. We’ve already standardized much of our lives around the convenient little connector, from phones and laptops to tablets and countless other gadgets. But for some reason, electric bikes have largely missed the memo. Now, though, I’m finally riding an e-bike that charges with USB-C, and the best part is that it doesn’t cost an arm and a leg.

Meet the ENGWE Zip, a quirky little folding electric bike that costs just €999 and has quickly become one of my favorite examples of how a small feature can make a big difference.

When it debuted earlier this year, it became only the third production e-bike I’ve seen that could charge via USB-C, allowing it to use the same charger that is likely already shared by your phone and laptop.

USB-C charging on electric bikes isn’t entirely new, but it’s surprisingly rare. Ampler was one of the first companies to introduce it barely a year ago, though its bikes are sadly no longer in production after the company’s bankruptcy. More recently, Rivian’s ALSO electric bike arrived with USB-C charging, but that bike costs around $4,500 – at least if you want the model that’s slowly starting to ship.

The ENGWE Zip, on the other hand, costs roughly a quarter as much as its only USB-charging competition. At €999, it’s priced at a relatively affordable US$1,100. That’s a quarter of the cost of the only other USB-C charging e-bike on the market.

Of course, it’s not nearly as technologically advanced as Rivian’s ALSO e-bike. But hey, it’s at least shipping.

And while the Zip is a fun little 16″ wheel folding electric bike in its own right, with a compact design that makes it easy to store and transport, it’s the charging setup that has me particularly excited.

Instead of keeping track of yet another proprietary charging brick, I can simply grab the USB-C charger from my laptop and plug it into the bike. There’s one in my living room by the couch. There’s one by my bed. There’s one in all of my friends’ places. There’s a USB-C charger everywhere.

If I’m traveling around, that means one less charger to pack. If I’m visiting someone, there’s a decent chance they already have a compatible charger sitting around.

Heck, I can even use a basic USB-C phone charger in a pinch. Sure, charging a relatively large e-bike battery at 20W isn’t going to be particularly quick, but the fact that I can do it at all is incredibly convenient.

Plus, the bike has one more trick. The battery also outputs USB-C, so I can charge my laptop or other devices from it as well. I can even charge two devices simultaneously, thanks to the dual USB-C ports.

The battery is housed in a roll-top bag that is locked into the headset of the bike but can be quickly unlocked for charging off the bike. And since it’s a keyed lock, no one can steal the battery even when the bag is left on the bike.

I typically charge the battery still mounted on the bike, though occasionally when I want to use a friend’s USB-C charger, I’ll just pop the bag off and bring it right up to wherever the closest USB-C charger is located.

It may not be the fastest charge, but it’s pretty darn convenient. And with a 360Wh battery, a powerful 100W laptop charger will still get it pretty much full in 4 hours, or for a more typical 50% recharge, roughly two hours.

And that’s really the beauty of USB-C charging. It’s not necessarily about charging faster. It’s about having options. It’s about not being stuck if the very specific charger that only works on your e-bike doesn’t happen to be around exactly where you are.

Of course, there’s a technical reason we haven’t seen USB-C charging spread across the e-bike industry quite as quickly as it has with smaller electronics. Most e-bike batteries operate at 36V or 48V nominal, meaning their charging voltages are higher than the 20V typically supplied by common USB-C laptop chargers. That requires additional voltage conversion and charging circuitry inside the bike or battery.

But clearly, it can be done. And if ENGWE can offer it on a €999 electric bike, there’s a pretty compelling argument that more manufacturers should be taking a serious look at the technology. In this case, it’s all housed inside the battery, meaning it could be directly incorporated into any e-bike whose manufacturer is brave enough to spec it.

USB-C charging aside, there's a very good reason that just about every folding e-bike on the market has put thick plates on the folding connection of the frame. It's because the frame breaks if they're not there. Just like this one is going to.

I’m not suggesting that every e-bike needs to abandon its dedicated charger tomorrow. For larger batteries, high-powered chargers still make plenty of sense, especially when you want to get back on the road quickly.

But having USB-C as an additional charging option? That’s something I’d love to see become standard.

For years, we’ve seen how electric bikes are becoming more convenient, more practical, and better integrated into our everyday lives. Yet when it comes to charging, we’re still carrying around a collection of more or less proprietary chargers.

Now I’m riding a barely $1k electric bike that can charge from the same power brick as my laptop. And frankly, I think it’s about time the rest of the e-bike industry caught up!

#4909. XRP Bulls and Bears to Get 3x ETFs Soon

Two proposed U.S. exchange-traded funds would give investors a way to bet on XRP in either direction, with one targeting three times XRP's daily return and the other targeting three times its inverse.

If XRP gains 5% in a single day, the bullish ETF would target a 15% gain, excluding fees and expenses.

If XRP loses 5% in a single day, the bearish ETF would target a 15% gain.

However, investors betting on the wrong direction could lose approximately 15% of their investment in a single day.

The next update is scheduled for Nov. 30. Following a recent amendment submitted to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the registration statements for these ETFs are now scheduled to become effective on Monday.

The issuer has repeatedly delayed the effective date. It remains to be seen whether the funds will start trading anytime soon.

The filing covers a total of eight ETFs, including bullish and bearish funds for Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH), Solana (SOL) and XRP.

Even if XRP's price remains unchanged over multiple trading days, both ETFs could record negative returns.

Since the ETFs rebalance daily, it's important to remember that when the price changes direction, the next day's percentage return is calculated based on the investment's value after the previous trading session.

Let's say XRP rises from $2 to $2.20 on Monday and then drops back to $2 on Tuesday. If you hold XRP over these two days, you'll break even.

However, if you invest $100 in the bullish ETF, your position would close Tuesday at approximately $94.55, assuming the fund achieves its daily target and excluding fees and expenses.

If XRP increases by 10% from $2 to $2.20 on Monday, the bullish ETF would target a 30% gain. Your initial $100 investment would now be worth $130.

For XRP to return to $2 on Tuesday, it would need to fall by approximately 9.09%.

The bullish ETF would therefore target a loss of roughly 27.27% on Tuesday. But that loss would be calculated against your $130 position, leaving you with approximately $94.55.

Of course, the bearish ETF wouldn't fare any better.

#4908. Tesla Cybercab’s autonomy agreement is insane: $299/mo or it doesn’t move

Tesla has posted the agreement that comes with its $29,990 Cybercab, and it’s even worse than the order page suggested. The two-seater can’t move without a $299 monthly “Autonomy Subscription” that Tesla can reprice with a month’s notice, suspend for a week, or cut off entirely.

And Tesla wants consumers to sign it while still refusing to give unsupervised self-driving to the Model Y owners it has been selling “Full Self-Driving” to for nearly a decade.

The “Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement” (version 20261112) went up on Tesla’s configurator late Friday, hours after the company started inviting select customers to order the Cybercab for personal use at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 per month.

The key line is short: “Your Cybercab will not operate without an active Autonomy Subscription.” There’s no steering wheel and no pedals, so that isn’t a figure of speech. Stop paying and you have a $30,000 object in your garage.

That personal-use clause kills the whole pitch. For years, Musk told people they’d buy a Tesla, add it to the fleet, and make money while they sleep. The first Tesla sold to consumers for unsupervised operation is contractually barred from doing exactly that.

Then there’s the geofence. Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas are already smaller in practice than advertised: when we tested them, real coverage was between 59% and 78% of the advertised maps, and parts of the Houston map have been called “fake” by the person tracking it. Now Tesla reserves the right to shrink that area after you’ve paid for the car.

Mark Valorian, who went through the terms on X, summed it up as “an endless variable-rate lease with a ridiculous down payment.” That’s about right.

Over five years, the car plus 59 paid months of subscription comes to $47,631 before insurance, registration, charging, and taxes, all of which are on the owner.

This is the part that should make every Tesla owner angry.

Tesla has spent the last year telling everyone that its Model Y is just as much a robotaxi as the Cybercab. Ahead of the Robotaxi launch in Austin, Musk said the cars were “the Model Ys we make currently, there’s no change to it.” On Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call last month, AI chief Ashok Elluswamy said Cybercabs and Model Y robotaxis already run the same software, and that customer cars might join the network around Q2 2027. The Cybercab launches on the same AI4 computer found in the current Model Y.

So the hardware is the same, the software is the same, and unsupervised Model Ys are already operating in the exact geofences where Cybercab owners will be allowed to ride.

Yet the people who paid for it get nothing. Tesla started selling “Full Self-Driving Capability” in 2016 on the promise that every car it built had the hardware for it. Owners paid up to $15,000 for the package. In February, Tesla stopped selling it outright and moved to a $99 per month subscription, which still requires you to supervise the car at all times.

Tesla’s answer to all those owners is a new car. One with two seats, no controls, a geofence it can move whenever it wants, and a subscription that costs three times as much as FSD.

I’ll say it plainly: this car is for suckers who want to give their money to Elon Musk.

You don’t own a Cybercab in any meaningful sense. You pay $30,000 for the right to keep paying Tesla $299 a month, at a price Tesla can raise, in an area Tesla can shrink, under rules Tesla enforces, with a camera pointed at you the whole time.

There are three possible reasons Tesla isn't allowing model Y owners to use FSD in the allowed zones:

1: the robotaxis are in fact different from the model Ys being sold

2: Tesla doesn't have enough "remote operators" to cover all of those supposedly self-driving cars if users join the network

3: Tesla isn't willing to accept liability when FSD kills someone.

And the Model Y part is what gives the game away. If Tesla truly believed its unsupervised system was ready for customers, the obvious move would be to turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin who already paid for it. It’s the same computer and the same software in the same geofence. But that would mean honoring a promise made in 2016, on cars already sold, with no new revenue attached.

A new vehicle wipes that slate clean. No legacy FSD buyers, no HW3 baggage, just a fresh customer locked into a $299 monthly fee from day one. What Tesla built is a subscription with a $30,000 entry fee attached to it.

So what happens the first time Tesla emails Cybercab owners a month’s notice that the price is going to $399?

#4907. Bitcoin Miners Go 98 Minutes Without Finding a Single Block

Bitcoin miners experienced their longest dry spell since July on Nov. 26. According to Galaxy's Alex Thorn, it took Bitcoin miners 98 minutes and 19 seconds to find the next block.

That's the third time in 2026 that miners have gone this long without finding a block. The wait ended at 18:28 UTC on Thursday.

For anyone trying to get Bitcoin transactions confirmed shortly after the previous block, the gap meant waiting more than an hour and a half.

Even if you paid a very high transaction fee, you would still have to wait until a miner found the next block before your transaction could receive its first confirmation.

Thursday's gap was the 69th longest since 2011, according to Galaxy Research. It was just three minutes shy of the threshold for the top 50.

And this year's other long gap lasted nearly two hours. On July 6, miners took 112 minutes and 26 seconds to find the next block (number 956,953). That was the 19th longest gap on record, according to Galaxy.

Bitcoin automatically adjusts mining difficulty every 2,016 blocks to keep the average block interval at around 10 minutes.

However,  blocks sometimes are found seconds apart. Other times, it takes well over an hour for the next block to be found.

At any given mining difficulty, the chance that a single attempt to find a block will succeed is incredibly small.

If miners have spent 90 minutes trying to find the next block, the chance of succeeding on the next attempt is the same as it was on the first attempt.

So the expected time until the next block is found is still 10 minutes, even if it's already been 90 minutes since the last block was found. That's assuming the network's total computing power and mining difficulty remain unchanged.

Assuming an average block interval of 10 minutes, Thorn said you could expect a gap of at least 98 minutes and 19 seconds about once every 18,600 block intervals.

That means such a gap should occur roughly once every four months, based on an average of about 144 blocks per day.

Galaxy examined 877,290 block intervals going back to Jan. 1, 2011.

Researchers identified 1,948 intervals where at least an hour had passed between the timestamps of successive blocks.

However, Galaxy flagged 97 of those intervals because an adjacent block had a timestamp that was off by at least 10 minutes. This raised questions about the actual length of those gaps.

The longest recorded interval is particularly interesting.

On Nov. 30, 2011, block 155,290 seemingly marked the end of a 144-minute-and-50-second gap.

However, the miner who found the next block had set its timestamp back by 65 minutes.

After excluding apparent timestamp errors, the longest gap was 141 minutes and one second, recorded on Oct. 13, 2011.

#4906. Ethereum Foundation Says AI Is a More Urgent Threat Than Quantum Computing

Ethereum Foundation Says AI Is a More Urgent Threat Than Quantum Computing

The Ethereum Foundation has doubled the size of its protocol security team and made strengthening Ethereum's cryptography its highest priority, warning that artificial intelligence could undermine the mathematical foundations of the network before quantum computers get powerful enough to do so.

"The EF has been planning mitigations to the threat posed by quantum computers," Kev Wedderburn wrote in a blog post published Monday, adding that "recently AI emerged as a more urgent risk."

For years, the crypto industry has worried about Q-Day—the hypothetical moment when quantum computers become powerful enough to break the cryptography protecting digital assets. AI introduces a different problem: What if someone discovers a mathematical shortcut that makes such a machine unnecessary?

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Ethereum with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Bitcoin and Ethereum both rely on elliptic curve cryptography to authenticate transactions. Its security depends on mathematical problems that are relatively easy to solve in one direction but prohibitively difficult to reverse using known algorithms.

An AI capable of discovering substantially better algorithms could change that equation without requiring any breakthroughs in quantum hardware.

Ethereum Foundation researcher Justin Drake raised this possibility in October, warning that existing signature schemes could become vulnerable within months rather than years under a worst-case scenario. He recommended that the industry start preparing for an orderly migration of funds to addresses whose public keys have never been exposed.

The Foundation's latest announcement comes just days after Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge and Claude produced a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, a mathematical problem that had remained unsolved since 1859.

The proof does not break Bitcoin or Ethereum's cryptography, but it illustrates how quickly AI is becoming useful in areas of mathematics previously considered beyond its capabilities.

The bug had survived roughly four years of scrutiny by cryptographers.

Ethereum's proposed solution involves moving away from elliptic curves and adopting hash-based cryptography. Hash functions turn data into fixed-length digital fingerprints that are designed to be extremely difficult to reverse, and their security relies on fewer structural mathematical assumptions than elliptic curve schemes.

Ethereum already depends on secure hash functions, making them an attractive foundation for its new security architecture.

The transition would affect how users authorize transactions, how validators secure the network, and how Ethereum verifies data submitted by layer-2 networks.

Developers are also pursuing formal verification, a technique that uses mathematical proofs to demonstrate that software behaves according to its specifications. Ironically, AI could help accelerate that work.

The Foundation has been deploying AI agents against its own infrastructure since earlier this year, successfully identifying software vulnerabilities before malicious actors could exploit them.

The security overhaul comes at a cost. Ethereum developers will need to rethink some planned features, and larger cryptographic signatures could increase hardware requirements for people running their own nodes.

Development group Ethlabs has already withdrawn its proposal to introduce faster block production in the upcoming Hegotá upgrade, freeing up engineering resources to pursue an ambitious target of making Ethereum resistant to both threats in 2027.

The Foundation previously established December 2029 as its internal deadline for achieving quantum resistance across Ethereum's base layer. Drake proposed bringing that target forward to December 2028 at the recent Devcon conference in Mumbai.

The Foundation plans to reassess its timeline in January 2027, with developers already testing early implementations of the new cryptographic infrastructure.

The financial community is uniting towards building the post-quantum cryptography (PQC) service, which would replace the algorithms prone to breaking by quantum computing. This aligns with the roadmap of several DLT-based altcoins, including Ripple (XRP) & Algorand (ALGO).

Both of these Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT) based chains are preparing for signatures that erases those threats, potentially fully implementing it by 2028. “Today’s cryptography is deeply embedded across systems, applications & processes”, – the paper states, carving out a transitional path.

Transitioning to new standards requires SWIFT compliant organisations to understand where they are exposed and manage change in a controlled, resilient way. Blockchain adoption comes as a no-brainer: SWIFT’s new ledger acts as a plug between multiple popular chains, including Ripple’s XRP.

However, that’s still pre-development aspirations.

Algorand’s better matched with SWIFT POC aspirations for now. XRP currently uses classical elliptic-curve signatures, known as secp256k1 / Ed25519. Santander, Standard Chartered, HSBC & Deutsche Bank are the highlights of a double-digit list, but that doesn’t necessarily mean XRP coin is used as collateral or settlement. The chain’s On-Demand Liquidity (ODL) provides an additional liquidity layer via XRP, but it’s optional.

#4904. Huawei set to challenge Tesla Powerwall with new, 20 kW home battery

This high-tech Huawei home battery pack hopes to hold back Tesla’s latest Powerwall with silicon carbide technology, AI-powered energy management baked in, and enough modular storage to keep even large homes bright and warm when the rest of the block goes dark.

Huawei believes its new Luterra S2 is more than just a home backup battery. The Chinese tech firm is calling it an “all-in-one residential energy system” that combines a hybrid inverter, modular battery storage, and AI-powered energy management in a single, simple, and stackable package that’s available in single-phase versions that put out between 3 and 10 kW and three-phase versions that can push up to 20 kW.

The Luterra S2 is the first system of its kind to use Huawei’s proprietary full-silicon carbide (SiC) architecture, which promises improved efficiency, power density, and ease of use. It’s so easy, in fact, that Huawei claims it can be installed and commissioned in just minutes.

“We are thrilled to introduce Huawei Luterra S2, our next-generation all-in-one residential energy system,” said Steve Zhang, President of Huawei Distributed PV & BESS Business. “By combining full-SiC architecture, AI-driven energy management, and industry-leading safety, Luterra S2 is designed to be smaller, lighter, quieter, safer, smarter and more powerful than ever before.”

Huawei’s basic Luterra S2 configuration starts with “just” 5 kWh of battery energy storage and 3 kW of output. That’s enough to keep essential household appliances, lighting, and electronics running during a power outage, but you’ll want to keep going if you’re preparing for more than a day or two without power.

If that sounds like you, Luterra’s got you covered. The modular system can be expanded with modular 7 kWh LFP battery packs and can scaling up to a massive 336 kWh of total storage across interconnected systems, with inverter output peaking at an impressive 60 kW using three 20 kW units in parallel.

Keeping all that power cool and quiet is a Huawei-developed passive cooling system that does without external fans, keeping operating noise levels below a claimed 29 dB (about the same as my Mac mini). It operates at ambient temperatures from –25° C to about 60° C, and features a sturdy IP66-rated enclosure (safe to hit with a high-pressure hose) with corrosion protection up to C5-M to keep it from rusting away.

Nice, but no mention of price or European availability.

Alas, the Luterra S2 probably won’t be making its way to the US anytime soon – but fear not! If you’re shopping for a Tesla Powerwall alternative that won’t help fund the absolute worst people in politics, there are a number of great home battery systems on the market that can deliver backup power, store your solar energy, and keep your home running when the grid goes down. #4903. Audiophiles are eating good this December with new headphones and earbuds from classic American brands

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 18, 2026 4:30 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

If you’re into personal audio, you might not want to spend all your money during Black Friday/Cyber Monday (but feel free to spend a little, and keep coming back here for some great suggestions as to how). Just within the last week, several innovative new headphones and earbuds have been announced, so read on for wired, wireless, and TWS options for every taste.

First up is Klipsch, the Hope, Arkansas-based heritage brand celebrating its 80th anniversary. But that doesn’t mean the acoustic design team is stuck in the past. Originally teased as Atlas at CES 2026 during a behind-closed-doors preview alongside powered standmount speakers and other surprises, the new Stratos Series uses an atypical (for headphones) two-way coaxial array, which aligns a mid/bass driver with a dynamic tweeter on a single axis to deliver low-distortion, high-efficiency, full-range sound.

The 380g Klipsch HP-2 (above) is the closed-back option, with a 40mm bio-cellulose woofer and 10mm tweeter achieving a frequency response of 15 Hz-18 kHz (+/-5 dB), plus isolation for more critical monitoring. The 458g HP-3 (below, and the one we’re most excited to audition) is a semi-open-back design that expands the woofer to 50mm to make up for some of the low end typically traded for a more expansive soundstage, and it achieves 16 Hz-22 kHz (+/-5 dB). Both promise “warm, punchy bass and crisp, sparkly highs,” and the pre-production units I heard in January delivered a good bright/bouncy balance, with rich, fun-colored but still composed mids as I recall (though it’s been many months removed).

Both models have an appropriately mid-century modern aesthetic, with auburn-stained sapele wood earcups and copper accents, machined aluminum yokes and contact points, Klipsch Heritage Twitchell grille cloth, replaceable microseude earpads, and protein-leather-wrapped open-cell-foam-filled headbands. Both 4.4mm balanced and 3.5mm unbalanced cables (plus a 1/4-inch adapter) with dual-mono connectors are included.

While both the Stratos HP-2 and HP-3 can be paired with smartphones and dongles of all sorts, they’ll really open up with a more refined signal chain, like the simultaneously announced $649.99 Onkyo HA-70, featuring two premium ESS ES9039Q2M SABRE DACs feeding an amplifier with plentiful inputs and three gain settings versatile enough to drive sensitive IEMs to 600Ω flagship headphones.

Compared to Klipsch, Brooklyn’s Grado Labs is a relatively young’un at the spry age of 73. First (and still) known for decades of producing phono cartridges, the family-owned company expanded into distinctive, hand-built headphones in the late ’80s (and still produces some fabulous flagships). The GW200 carries that tradition into something you can carry. The 235g GW200 takes a 44m S paper-composite diaphragm derived from the drivers in the company’s multi-thousand-dollar Signature line and puts it in an open-back wireless headphone. This helps deliver expressive bass and treble articulation within a frequency response of 16Hz – 34kHz.

Being open-back means a more spacious presentation with more instrument separation than your typical Bluetooth headphone (at the expense of isolation, of course, so don’t expect these to stand in for ANC travel headphones). Helping ensure this is Bluetooth 5.4 with support for Qualcomm aptX Lossless, aptX Adaptive, aptX HD, aptX, AAC, and SBC, plus 60+ hours of battery life. And there’s a single-sided 3.5mm audio input for passive use in case the battery does run out (or you just prefer an external DAC/amp combo).

As for comfort and tuning, the GW200 comes with the Grado Labs F Cushions but is compatible with Grado’s complete line, so you can change both the physical and sonic feel by swapping them. Another trickle-down from the Signature series is the padded leather headband, which goes nicely with the matte black finish. We’re looking forward to getting a pair to try out.

Over in eastern Texas, Noble Audio has been producing artisan IEMs since the early 2010s (and founder John Moulton was doing custom in-ear monitors for enthusiasts even before that). In recent years, the company has been showing what’s possible when the multiple-driver mentality of IEMs (some costing many thousands of dollars) is turned to portable audio, and the Astrid is the latest example. A tribrid architecture featuring an 8.3mm dynamic driver with a PU diaphragm and an aluminum-magnesium alloy dome, a 6mm planar driver, and one balanced armature in each earpiece, the Astrid brings a wired configuration and sophistication to true wireless earbuds.

The overall tonality of the Astrid is rich, full-bodied, but not boomy … punch but not paunch. While sitting beneath the company’s top TWS model, the 4-driver Prestige Encore, Astrid still delivers a detailed soundstage. What really brings the best out of it is the Audiodo Personal Sound feature, which uses a short tone recognition test to test each ear and saves per-channel adjustments on the earbuds to make up for any anatomically incurred frequency range deficiencies. Then Audiodo Equalizer lets you address sensitivities/preferences, overlaying further adjustments on your personalized curve (3-band on iOS, 5-band on Android). There’s also an assessment-independent 10-band EQ if that level of control is more your vibe.

To ensure the most cohesive playback possible, there’s multipoint Bluetooth 6.0 with high-resolution LDAC/aptX Adaptive support for compatible devices, as well as AAC and SBC. Plus active noise cancellation. Battery life is rated up to 11 hours on a single charge, with the wireless/USB-C case bringing the total carry capacity to 40 hours. All that is wrapped in IPX4 ABS enclosures featuring “divinely beautiful” glass fiber faceplates adorned with a dense lattice of silver filigree, like electro-acoustic etching … a metallic polyphony of colliding chords and intersecting transients.

#4902. Crypto bridge hacks can spread losses far beyond the assets they compromise

Recent exploits expose how broken redemption mechanisms, fragmented liquidity and compromised collateral can spread losses across DeFi lending markets.

Multichain’s version of USDC on Fantom was at nearly $0.12 on Nov. 25, more than three years after the bridge that backed it failed, while the Circle-issued USDC and the version bridged to Arbitrum were at $0.9996 each.

Recent bridge exploits at Fusionist and Cyber show how quickly a token can lose the backing or conversion route that held its price close to the original. Buyers can still find a price on a screen even as their options for converting or selling the token shrink.

A bridge lets a token circulate on a blockchain where it was never issued. A US bankruptcy court account describes how Multichain let users lock Ethereum USDC on one side and receive a representation they could later convert back.

In July 2023, Chainalysis traced unauthorized withdrawals that included USDC from Multichain’s Fantom bridge. Multichain announced that bridge service was stopping indefinitely and later said it had ceased operations. On Fantom, the damage reached lender Geist Finance, which stopped operating after taking losses.

On Nov. 25, the USDC version on Fantom was 88.18% below $1, with about $2,472 in reported daily trading volume. Circle-issued USDC and Arbitrum’s USDC.e were both 0.04% below $1, with daily volume of about $15 billion across the native listing and $2.1 million for the Arbitrum wrapper.

CoinGecko quotes (in US dollars) per token at about 18:38 UTC on Nov. 25. Circle-issued USDC and Arbitrum USDC.e were each $0.9996, while Multichain USDC on Fantom was $0.1182.

Source: Circle USDC · · Arbitrum USDC.e · · Fantom USDC

DEX Screener quoted the same Fantom token at $0.04 in SpookySwap’s USDC/WFTM pool, which held about $94,000 in assets, roughly half on the WFTM side.

Eligible Circle Mint customers can redeem native USDC for dollars under Circle’s terms, while Arbitrum’s canonical bridge locks Ethereum USDC and issues USDC.e on Arbitrum.

A holder who converts a bridged token must get the underlying asset back before asking the issuer to convert it to dollars. For specified third-party versions, Circle’s bridged USDC terms make conversion dependent on the available bridge and network.

Georges Chouchani, founder and CEO of Euclid Protocol, told CryptoSlate:

“As long as people believe they can redeem one-for-one, someone will buy the copy at 99 cents and redeem it at a dollar.”

The buyer pockets the difference after fees and other conversion costs, and those purchases can pull the cheaper token toward par. They also depend on the bridge honoring the conversion and the trader being able to complete it.

New York Fed researchers looked at hourly prices for native and bridged USDC and USDT across a selection of networks in the first three quarters of 2024, finding an average correlation of 0.381.

The researchers interpreted the imperfect alignment as evidence that moving value between chains can introduce enough friction to obstruct the law of one price, the idea that equivalent claims should trade at the same price.

Circle reported $3.3 billion of reserves at Silicon Valley Bank in March 2023, and Federal Reserve Board staff found that USDC traded below $0.90 before recovering over about three days.

On Nov. 22, Fusionist’s wrapped ACE fell from about $0.12 to less than one millionth of a dollar in about an hour on BNB Chain, according to Bitquery’s analysis of decentralized exchange trades.

Traders bought the discounted tokens and attempted to convert them back to ACE on Fusionist’s Endurance chain. Bitquery counted approvals for roughly 53.7 million ACE to return and estimated that backing fell to 148 ACE based on the bridge’s BNB Chain records.

Buying a cheap token to convert it would normally pull the prices closer together. In this case, the bridge kept approving conversions after unbacked tokens had entered circulation.

Every completed conversion would take more assets from the vault, leaving less backing for the next holder and making the price gap harder to close.

Gate announced a rollback for ACE/USDT spot trades on its exchange between 17:55 and 19:15 UTC on Nov. 22. Bithumb announced a temporary trading suspension after it had already paused ACE transfers.

On Nov. 24, Fusionist said it was coordinating recovery with exchanges and would share a timeline when it had one. An ACE holder could see a price in a decentralized pool and still face a suspension or potential trade reversal on a centralized venue.

The day before the Fusionist breach, Bitquery traced the issuance of 5,213,000 unbacked CYBER on Solana and the release of the same amount, worth about $1.1 million, from the bridge’s Ethereum vault.

In its Nov. 24 update, Cyber said it had burned an equivalent amount from team and treasury allocations and that the bridge was still temporarily suspended.

The options had already split at Bithumb, where customers could trade existing CYBER balances even after the exchange paused deposits and withdrawals.

“If you have $1 million of liquidity on each of 10 chains, $10 million exists, but a trader on any one chain can only reach $1 million of it.”

What is key for an order is the pool or venue the trader can reach. CoinGecko’s sample showed $33.8 million in reported sell-side depth within 2% for native USDC against USDT on Binance. The same measure for USDC.e against USDT0 on Curve Arbitrum was about $12,231.

Hyperbridge reported an unauthorized mint of about 1 billion bridged DOT. Its initial $237,000 loss estimate covered the immediately visible Ethereum selloff, but after reviewing four affected chains and related incentive pools, Hyperbridge revised the total to about $2.5 million in realized losses.

Chouchani pointed to lending collateral as a route for losses to reach people who never held the compromised token. In April’s Kelp bridge breach, 116,500 rsETH tokens valued at about $292 million were released.

The Aave incident report documented using some of those tokens as collateral to borrow other assets before the protocol froze affected reserves.

If the collateral can no longer be sold for enough to cover the loan, the lending market faces a shortfall. Aave’s report modeled different possible losses depending on how the damage would be allocated.

In this case, the lending market was exposed as soon as it let users borrow other assets against the compromised token, and people who supplied those other assets could bear some of the cost.

Network and contract address help identify who issued the token and which bridge stands between the holder and the underlying asset. Circle’s bridged USDC standard provides a route for eligible deployments to upgrade to native issuance by mutual agreement.

Chouchani said that a design with fewer wrapped tokens can concentrate risk in whatever coordinates settlement across chains. He pointed to smart contracts, validator assumptions, and what happens when one chain takes longer to finalize a transfer.

“No cross-chain design is free of risk, ours included.”

For a specific token, check where the backing is held, whether conversion is operating, and who can use it.

Then check the price available for the amount you want to sell, and what happened the last time trading or withdrawals came under stress.

A token can share the original’s ticker and trade at the same price on a normal day. The contract, conversion terms, and available market tell the investors what that price buys.

#4901. Check your ego at the door: Stellantis’ new electric dolly turns ANY car into a tow rig

We all know the type: grizzled stubble, wraparound PitVipers, a MAGA hat quietly retired after last week’s deep-blue shellacking, and a pristine, polished pickup parked in the driveway that they “need for towing.” With Stellantis’ new patent for an AI-powered electric tow dolly that turns just about ANY vehicle into a capable tow rig, however, those might need a new to find a new excuse to keep that gas-guzzler.

Originally filed in 2023, Stellantis received US Patent No. 12,779,916 for its electric tow dolly on 03NOV2026. The patent covers a machine that’s designed to shoulder the trailer’s hitch load with its own ball hitch or fifth-wheel plate, using an on-board electric motor and battery to get the trailer going while its regenerative braking system and AI-backed steering and traction control system keeps everything pointed in the right direction.

In other words, the dolly takes on many of the jobs that traditionally require a big tow vehicle: providing the pulling power, managing the trailer’s weight and controlling its braking and traction. The vehicle up front doesn’t necessarily need a massive motor, heavy-duty suspension or oversized brakes. With a system like this, you could argue that the “tow vehicle” isn’t really a tow vehicle at all. It’s more of a “lead vehicle,” since the dolly is the one doing the towing … and it can follow just about anything – including the diminutive (and supremely affordable) Fiat 500e, which is also made by Stellantis.

To be clear, this isn’t just Uncle Jojo making fun of the commuter conveys – Stellantis’ patent describes the dolly as being equipped with an autonomous control system using cameras, sensors, a controller, and an advanced, four wheel steer-by-wire system. It also specifically discusses how the dolly’s independently powered acceleration, braking and steering, and sway controls essentially remove the need to own a truck in the first place.

The dolly system’s truck bed sides and small size allow users to experience the functionality and utility of a truck only when they need it, allowing them to own a smaller, cheaper, and more fuel efficient vehicle that suits daily use needs.

There are some pretty obvious practical questions still to answer, of course, including how much battery capacity the dolly would need, how much weight it could handle and how it would perform on long grades or in emergency braking situations. And, to be clear, a patent isn’t a product announcement or proof that Stellantis plans to put one of these things on sale – heck, if I were Stellantis’ CEO, I’d patent this thing just to prevent anyone else from building one so I could keep selling ancient, low-tech, high-margin Ram Trucks – but it’s a neat idea.

Okay, I like this idea and appreciate the problem it is trying to solve, but it has the same challenge as any electric-tow situation, which is the charging logistics. Even if you find a pull-through charger (very rare), if you are using an EV, you still need to charge two "vehicles," so you have to charge your car, then pull up and charge the dolly afterwards. Even if you are using a gas car, charging the dolly will be logistically challenging. Of course, that's a problem with an easy solution (more pull-through chargers), but also one that doesn't seem to be on any charging network's radar.

I think it’s neat, anyway. What do you guys think? Are you ready to trade in your big-battery Chevy Silverado EV or Volvo VNR 800 on a new Topolino, or are you going to keep driving inefficient 99% of the time? Let us know, in the comments.

#4900. Bitcoin’s recovery hinges on a US economic slowdown without a recession

Cooling inflation and resilient employment could ease pressure from the Fed, but deteriorating consumer demand threatens to undermine crypto’s recovery.

Real disposable income for US households rose 0.5% from September, the Bureau of Economic Analysis said in its Nov. 25 income and spending report, and this can impact Bitcoin over the next three months.

Slower inflation could persuade investors that the Federal Reserve has fewer rate increases ahead, while steady hiring and spending could keep them willing to take risk.

If traders expect fewer hikes because they fear a steep economic downturn, demand for Bitcoin could weaken alongside other risk assets.

The October income and spending figures show that personal income rose 0.7% in current dollars, and disposable income rose 0.8% after taxes. The 0.5% real gain measures what that extra income could buy. Real spending fell by less than 0.1%, which the BEA rounded to 0.0% in its table.

In September, real disposable income had fallen 0.2% while real spending rose 0.1%.

October real spending edged down by less than 0.1%. Bars show monthly changes after inflation in the BEA’s Nov. 25 release.

Source: BEA November 25 release · BEA data tables (PDF)

The saving rate was 4.1% in October, as higher private wages and salaries and more dividend income helped lift personal income. One-time Medicare premium rebate payments also contributed. That temporary boost makes it harder to judge how much of October’s gain will carry into future months.

The aggregate spending and income figures can describe the split without telling us whether households saved more because they felt cautious.

The BEA raised third-quarter growth to 4.3% annually from 3.4%, mainly after revising investment and consumer spending higher. The October spending figure offers a first look at a later period, so strong quarterly growth and a weak spending month can coexist.

Headline PCE inflation slowed to 0.3% on the month from 0.5% in September and stood at 3.8% year over year. Core PCE, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.3% for a second straight month and 3.3% from a year earlier.

At that monthly core pace, core prices would rise about 3.7% over a full year after compounding. A series of cooler core readings would give investors more grounds to expect the Fed to stop tightening.

On Nov. 5, the US two-year Treasury yield fell 12 basis points, from 4.58% the previous day to 4.46%. Over the same period, Bitcoin fell from $80,420.06 to $76,152.52, about 5.3%, while the Nasdaq Composite fell about 5.5%.

The two-year yield reflects where investors expect short-term rates to go, among other factors. It can fall because price pressures are easing, or because investors see enough economic risk to seek safer assets and expect a weaker economy to limit the Fed’s next moves.

A drop in yields alongside broad selling gives little comfort if investors are cutting exposure to assets that depend on confidence and ready liquidity.

Bitcoin could begin recovering before the Fed finishes hiking, since investors price assets based on where they think rates are headed, so a credible shift toward a lower expected peak or a shorter period of restrictive rates can matter before a policy decision.

Cooler inflation with solid hiring and steady spending would give that shift a firmer footing, while falling yields alongside worsening job and spending data would tell a different story.

The central bank held its target rate at 3.75% to 4% on Oct. 28, with two dissenters favoring a quarter-point increase. In minutes released Nov. 18, almost all participants judged that further hikes would likely be appropriate under their baseline outlooks for inflation and employment.

The Fed’s September projections offer one picture of inflation easing alongside continued expansion. The median participant projection put core PCE inflation at 2.5% in 2027, down from 3.4% in 2026, with the projected year-end policy rate at 4.1% in both years.

The 2027 medians also included 2.4% real GDP growth and 4.1% unemployment. A lower inflation forecast can coexist with rates staying elevated well into 2027, and Bitcoin can respond sooner if the new data lead investors to expect a different path.

If purchasing power continues to grow and spending expands modestly, businesses could face less pressure to raise prices even as demand holds up.

If income gains turn into a surge in spending, inflation could stay high and bring more tightening into view.

If demand falls sharply, the damage to risk appetite could outweigh the benefit of fewer expected hikes. Persistent inflation combined with weakening growth would constrain the Fed and put both sources of pressure on Bitcoin at once.

Cooling inflation and a growth scare can both lower rate expectations. The starting conditions shape risk appetite.

Cooling prices with steady hiring and demand could give Bitcoin room to recover before the Fed’s last hike.

The Nov. 5 Treasury yield, Bitcoin and Nasdaq readings use different market clocks. The scenarios illustrate how growth conditions can affect Bitcoin.

Aligned, non-directional lines keep each illustrative scenario in its own lane. The band marks a change in rate expectations that is possible in either case. No geometry encodes magnitude, timing or probability.

The Nov. 5 Treasury yield, Bitcoin and Nasdaq readings use different market clocks. The scenarios illustrate how growth conditions can affect Bitcoin.

Farside Investors’ daily fund flows show the US spot Bitcoin funds it tracks recorded aggregate net withdrawals in all six completed trading sessions from Nov. 17 through Nov. 24.

Glassnode’s spot-market analysis found aggressive sellers outweighed buyers on Coinbase over its 30-day window. A string of ETF inflows and renewed spot buying would together make a better case for a sustained recovery than a price rebound on its own.

More stablecoins in circulation can mean more liquidity in crypto markets, so a rise in supply gives investors a reason to look for stronger buying in Bitcoin itself. If Bitcoin rallies after a softer inflation report, look for follow-through in fund flows and spot activity after the initial trading burst.

The December economic calendar will test whether the other half of the recovery case is taking shape. The Nov. 6 employment report showed October payrolls rising by 165,000 and unemployment little changed at 4.1%.

The next jobs report, scheduled for Dec. 4, will show whether that resilience is holding. The Fed’s Dec. 8-9 meeting brings updated projections, and the new estimates will give investors a fresh policy baseline for 2027.

They can compare that path with what two-year yields and rate futures imply and watch how equities respond.

An orderly moderation in hiring could be consistent with the slowdown Bitcoin needs, while a much weaker report paired with falling equities would give a drop in yields a different meaning.

The Dec. 23 PCE release will show how inflation, purchasing power, and real spending moved in the same month. Together, those readings will help frame the Fed’s next meeting, tentatively set for Jan. 26-27.

If those reports show inflation slowing while jobs and spending hold up, the next test is whether Bitcoin buyers stick around after the initial price reaction. A run of ETF inflows and better spot demand would give a rebound more staying power.

#4899. Shiba Inu (SHIB) Dev Reveals Bi-Fold Shibarium Revamp

#4898. Coldcard Bitcoin Exploit, Revisited: How a Hidden Flaw Survived Years of Audits

Coldcard Bitcoin Exploit, Revisited: How a Hidden Flaw Survived Years of Audits

Four months after attackers drained Bitcoin from compromised Coldcard hardware wallets, the device’s maker has published a detailed autopsy of how a single configuration error went undetected for more than five years, slipping past at least 15 separate security reviews before thieves exploited it.

The postmortem, released Monday by manufacturer Coinkite and modeled on an NTSB accident report, confirms the core failure when the exploit surfaced in July: from March 2021 through July 2026, Coldcard firmware generated wallet seeds using a software pseudo-random number generator, MicroPython’s Yasmarang, instead of the device’s intended hardware random-number generator.

The result was seeds with roughly 40 to 72 bits of effective randomness rather than the 128-bit target, weak enough for attackers to regenerate private keys offline and steal funds without ever touching a device.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The new report’s most revealing section is its accounting of why the flaw hid for so long.

Coinkite documented at least 15 independent review efforts between 2021 and 2026, including two paid third-party audits, physical-security work by Ledger Donjon, and even an AI-assisted firmware review that produced 85 findings. None caught it.

As the report puts it, every check “answered a nearby question rather than the critical one”: release checks confirmed the hardware-RNG code was present, but not that seed generation actually reached it, and statistical tests couldn’t distinguish the defective generator’s output from a properly seeded one.

A safeguard meant to reject the faulty configuration, a guard in the underlying libNgU code, simply didn’t work.

The scale of losses remains murky. Coinkite said it has received about 300 loss-related support tickets tied to 242 accounts, roughly 0.21% of its estimated user base, while Galaxy Research has attributed more than 8,600 addresses to the theft. The company cautions that those figures count different things and can’t be combined into a victim total.

One thread running through the report is the role of AI. Coinkite notes the first thefts began just two days after the Kimi K3 model’s full weights were released, calling AI-assisted discovery “a plausible hypothesis, not an attribution.”

It also documents how, after the flaw went public, the Bitcoin Red Team used Kimi K3 to run a 108-hour multi-model sweep that flagged nearly 8,000 candidate findings across 501 Bitcoin projects, underscoring how AI has upended the economics of vulnerability hunting.

Coinkite has since rebuilt its seed generation, adding mandatory user entropy, multiple hardware sources, and build-time and boot-time checks, with an independent review by Keylabs concluding the defect is “fully closed” in current standard firmware.

But no update repairs seeds already created on affected devices; those users must migrate to new ones. The report ends with a plea to whoever holds the stolen Bitcoin: return it.

“Some victims lost life-changing amounts, and returning the funds is the only action that can directly reduce that harm,” the company said.

#4897. Rare rhino birth caught on camera at England’s Chester Zoo

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 18, 2026 7:01 PM EST

On the evening of October 11, a rare greater one-horned rhinoceros (Rhinoceros unicornis) was born at the Chester Zoo in England. Even more exciting, CCTV cameras captured the poignant moment for this threatened species. The footage shows rhino mom Asha giving birth, and the calf’s first unsure steps into the world.

The sex and weight have not been announced yet, and the calf also does not have a name.

At birth, greater one-horned rhino calves weigh about 100 pounds. By comparison, the largest adult greater one-horned rhinos weigh over two tons, or as much as a car.

The team used a combination of experience and non-invasive testing to help plan out the pregnancy. They closely monitored Asha’s behavior and regularly collected samples of her poop. By testing hormone levels in the samples, they could track Asha’s reproductive cycle and identify when she would be most open to mating. This helped the team safely introduce her to Beni the rhino, while a separate analysis helped confirm the pregnancy.

“Asha was pregnant for about 15 months, so it’s a long wait! We had our fingers crossed when she showed signs of labour and we knew we were likely to welcome the calf very soon,” Emma Evison, Team Manager for rhinos said in an e-mailed statement. “It was a big moment for us—and for the conservation breeding programme—when the calf arrived. Any birth can be risky, even for an experienced mum, but fortunately everything went smoothly. The calf was up and about within an hour and feeding shortly afterwards. Asha knows exactly what she’s doing.”

Both mother and calf are reportedly in good health. They remained inside for the first few days following the birth to stay warm, but are now venturing to a special behind-the-scenes paddock outside of the enclosure. The calf is Asha’s fourth with father Beni. Sadly, Beni died in September following a sudden and brief illness.

“Beni was a lovely rhino. He was calm and approachable, helped train animal care specialists and even took part in animal behaviour studies,” added Tom Garland, Assistant Manager of the rhino team at Chester Zoo. “It’s lovely to know that his legacy lives on through this calf.”

While not the largest rhino species in the world, greater one-horned rhinos stand about six feet tall at the shoulder and are the biggest in Asia. They have the smallest horns of any rhino, but also have the biggest teeth. The males will sometimes use these chompers to bite each other while sparring. Currently, about 4,000 greater one-horned rhinos are alive today. They live in India and Nepal, in forests, wetlands, and grasslands. In the early 1990s, trophy hunting and habitat loss almost drove them to extinction.. Poaching for their prized horns also threatened their survival.

While the IUCN Red List of Endangered Species currently lists them as Vulnerable, they remain  at risk of extinction. Many of the rhinos are concentrated into a relatively small number of protected areas, putting their genetic diversity at risk. A lack of genetic diversity can lead to inbreeding and worse health outcomes in general. This new calf is part of a Europe-wide conservation breeding program to help maintain a healthy and genetically diverse population of greater one-horned rhinos living in human care.

“Supporting Asha’s pregnancy has been really exciting,” added conservation scientist John O’Hanlan. “She’s one of relatively few greater one-horned rhinos in Europe actively breeding, so every successful birth is important in maintaining a healthy and genetically diverse population.”

#4896. $20K Nissan NX7 PHEV goes on sale with nearly 200 miles of electric range

Dongfeng Nissan officially opened the early order book on its new NX7 hybrid yesterday, promising up to 320 km (~198 miles) of all-electric range from a 40 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery and a $20,000 price tag.

When the first generation Nissan LEAF bowed with 70-ish miles of range from its 24 kWh li-ion battery pack, it struggled to meet widespread adoption, especially in an SUV-obsessed US market that demands forethought-free trips to Home Depot and bladder-busting range. The company’s latest 2027 Rogue Hybrid is a step in the right direction, using a gas engine to generate electricity for a pair of electric drive motors that deliver a driving experience that’s remarkably similar to a “pure” electric car – but without a plug, it’s still entirely dependent on fossil fuels. The new Dongfeng Nissan NX7, though? That’s a different story.

The plug-in hybrid Dongfeng Nissan NX7 might be called a “long range hybrid” in the same sense that Volvo’s Euro-market XC70 is, in that it’s an EV for the 360-odd days a year that you’re driving less than 200 miles, and an ICE vehicle for the handful of days you drive more. And if you’re one of those people who thinks stopping on road trips is a character flaw, a fully charged and topped off NX7 will take you an astonishing 1,666 km (~1,035 miles) from where you started.

The new NX7 could be an ideal lilypad vehicle for North American drivers who are either too afraid of being caught without a charger or too invested in the outcome of one or more dumb oil wars to confidently make the switch to EV – and, even at twice the 129,900 yuan ($~19,400) asking price, I think it would be a hit.

For that money, NX7 buyers get an absolutely loaded Model Y-sized crossover (they’re within 1/4″ of each other in length), with a 17.3″ central touchscreen, a fully digital instrument cluster, and (on higher-spec models) a positively massive 55″ augmented-reality head-up display powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8295P automotive processor and running on Nissan OS 3.0 with an AI-powered voice assistant developed with iFlytek that, Nissan claims, can recognize natural-language commands, remember user preferences, and even recognize occupants, adjusting vehicle settings accordingly.

On top-shelf models, the NX7 cabins get “AI Zero-Pressure Cloud Blanket” seats that use sensors and air-cushion arrays to dynamically adjust for maximum comfort, and include heating, ventilation, and a 12-point SPA-level massage function. The front seats can be fully reclined to create a bed-like configuration that will be familiar to Cube owners. The NX7 even offers an on-board refrigerator and motion-sickness prevention system that Nissan claims can reduce motion sickness by as much as 83% (which, like, I wouldn’t want to be the one to test that – but seems cool).

Power comes from a 1.5-liter naturally aspirated internal combustion engine making 98 hp that’s paired to a 228 hp electric drive motor and the previously mentioned 40.9 kWh LFP battery. It’s not immediately clear if the NX7 uses a conventional parallel hybrid system like a Prius or a series-hybrid-plus-plug setup, but Dongfeng’s hybrid technology patents describe a pretty versatile arrangement with four possible operating modes: series hybrid, parallel hybrid, direct engine drive and electricity generation – which means the vehicle can theoretically use the ICE motor as a generator, drive the wheels mechanically, or work alongside the electric motor, depending on what the operating conditions call for. Whether any or all four modes make it to production on the NX7 remains to be seen, but it’s an intriguing bit of engineering for a vehicle promising nearly 200 miles of electric driving range.

Why is this article written like it will be available in the US market? It’s made in China and has Chinese software, we’ll never see it

The final production version will be shown to the public for the first time at the Guangzhou Auto Show later this month, but you can let us know what you think of the new NX7 in the comments, today.

#4895. US government could be barred from selling its strategic Bitcoin holdings for 20 years

Legislation awaiting House passage would establish long-term holding requirements alongside public verification of Treasury's Bitcoin reserves.

The US Treasury could be required to publicly verify its Bitcoin holdings under legislation advancing through Congress.

The House Financial Services Committee formally reported the amended American Reserve Modernization Act of 2026 on Nov. 24, placing it on the House Union Calendar for the full chamber to consider.

The legislative development follows the committee's Sept. 16 vote, when lawmakers approved the measure 28-21.

Introduced in May by Republican Rep. Nick Begich, the bill would give statutory backing to the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve that President Donald Trump established through a March 2025 executive order.

Under Section 6 of the legislation, Treasury would establish a proof-of-reserves system using public cryptographic attestations and publish annual reports detailing its Bitcoin holdings, transactions, and control of the associated private keys.

Treasury would also appoint an independent auditor specializing in cryptographic attestations to verify the accuracy of its disclosures. The US Comptroller General would regularly review the reserve's management and audits.

The proposed requirements would give investors a clearer picture of how much Bitcoin the federal government has accumulated as a strategic asset.

Trump's executive order required federal agencies to account for their digital asset holdings within 30 days, but directed those disclosures to Treasury and the President's Working Group on Digital Asset Markets rather than the public.

H.R. 8957 would require a broad internal agency inventory and a public report on Bitcoin deposited in the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve.

The annual public report would detail reserve holdings, transactions and control of private keys.

The bill leaves the cryptographic proof method open. Court and forfeiture records would remain relevant to title and third-party claims.

Maps the roles of Sections 3, 4, 6 and 7 of H.R. 8957, along with the third-party claim process in 21 U.S.C. § 853(n).

The bill leaves the cryptographic proof method open. Court and forfeiture records would remain relevant to title and third-party claims.

The distinction is significant because government-linked blockchain wallets can contain seized Bitcoin that remains subject to legal proceedings or restitution claims. Cryptographic verification, combined with independent accounting, could help establish how much Bitcoin actually belongs to the reserve.

Beyond transparency, the legislation would formalize the federal government's long-term Bitcoin accumulation strategy and limit its ability to liquidate reserve assets.

Federal agencies would have 60 days after enactment to submit comprehensive inventories of their cryptocurrency holdings to Treasury.

The department would then have six months from enactment to establish the statutory Bitcoin reserve and a separate stockpile for other digital assets. Agencies would have another 30 days to transfer eligible holdings.

Federally owned Bitcoin deposited into the reserve would face a minimum 20-year holding period beginning at enactment, during which Treasury could neither sell the assets nor pledge them as collateral.

Two years before that period expires, Treasury would recommend whether to continue holding Bitcoin or begin gradually reducing its position. Potential sales could reach 10% of reserve assets over any two-year period following the lockup.

Meanwhile, the legislation directs the Treasury and Commerce departments to evaluate ways of expanding the reserve without increasing the national debt or imposing additional costs on taxpayers.

The six-month study would examine potential exchanges of other government-held cryptocurrencies for Bitcoin, additional asset forfeitures and partnerships with states, private entities and international counterparts.

However, the legislation faces a tightening congressional timetable. With the 119th Congress approaching its January conclusion, lawmakers have limited time to secure House and Senate approval.

Failure to pass the measure before the current Congress ends would require its reintroduction in the next session, leaving America's Bitcoin reserve governed by executive action without the proposed public auditing requirements.

#4894. China’s electric airliner era starts with a 19-seat plane and 400 km of range

COMAC’s CE-25A, China’s 19-seat battery-electric commuter plane, flew with a crew for the first time on Saturday in Binzhou, Shandong. Two pilots and a flight test engineer were aboard the roughly 10-tonne demonstrator, and COMAC says every system worked normally.

It wasn’t the plane’s first flight. The CE-25A had already completed 19 autonomous test flights with nobody on board since February 2, and China’s aviation regulator is now reviewing it for a type certificate.

The CE-25A is a T-tail commuter plane with 10 electric ducted fans on the wings, five per side, instead of propellers. COMAC lists a 300 km/h cruise speed and a 400 km (250-mile) range.

The CAAC accepting COMAC’s type certificate application starts the airworthiness review. It doesn’t mean paying passengers are close, and COMAC hasn’t given a date for commercial service.

The program has been quiet for a long time. COMAC showed a CE-25A model at the China International Import Expo in Shanghai in November 2023, with a placard listing 400 to 500 km of range and a 400 km/h top cruise speed. The full-size aircraft, registered B-0EFH, only became public when photos leaked on Chinese social media on October 28.

The obvious battery candidate is CATL. In July 2023, COMAC, CATL, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University formed a joint venture with CNY 600 million in registered capital to develop electric aircraft, as we reported when CATL launched its aviation unit.

CATL had just unveiled its “condensed” battery at the time, claiming up to 500 Wh/kg at the cell level, and said it was testing the cells to aviation standards. Neither company has confirmed what’s inside the CE-25A, though.

~500 Wh/kg has long been seen as the target for battery energy density to enable electric flight on a commercial scale.

COMAC isn’t alone in flying a large electric demonstrator. In August, Heart Aerospace flew its X1 in Plattsburgh, New York, for 27 minutes. It’s a 25,000-lb aircraft with a 106-foot wingspan, which Heart calls the largest battery-electric aircraft ever flown.

Eviation flew its 9-passenger Alice back in September 2022, then laid off most of its staff in early 2025.

Heart is the closest Western comparison. It dropped its 19-seat ES-19 for the 30-seat ES-30 back in 2022, and the ES-30 now relies on reserve turbogenerators to stretch its range, with BAE Systems working on the battery. Heart is targeting 2031 for service and claims “more than 40%” lower operating costs.

For years, the go-to excuse in the West for doing nothing about emissions was China. Why should we bother, the argument went, if China won’t? Now China is pulling ahead, and it’s doing it by cutting its dependence on fossil fuels.

Look at trucking. Electric trucks hit 50.3% of China’s heavy truck sales in September, and they’re already eating into the country’s diesel demand. In the US, electric models were about 0.3% of heavy-truck sales last year, according to the ICCT.

A great step in the right direction, probably needs a doubling in range but at current rates of progress that will only be five years away.

Now it’s planes, starting where batteries make sense today: short regional routes. The CE-25A’s 400 km shrinks once you keep the reserves regulators require, and a Beechcraft 1900 turboprop in the same class covers well over 1,000 km. So it’s not replacing turboprops anytime soon. But that’s how trucking started too. Short-haul first, then long-haul tractors once the batteries caught up.

And this couldn’t happen fast enough. We’re in the middle of a diesel and jet fuel crisis. Jet fuel averaged $3.50 a gallon in early August, up 63% from a year earlier, according to Heart Aerospace. Every truck and plane China moves to batteries is one less exposed to that.

China also has the batteries to pull it off, with CATL in the joint venture. Meanwhile, Heart has pushed to 2031 and added a fuel-burning backup, and Eviation is a cautionary tale.
